questions.stem: Selective attention is the ability to:
options: focus on one stimulus while ignoring other stimuli
attend to two or more different tasks at the same time
maintain focus on a task over a long period
process sensory information without any awareness
questions.explanation: Selective attention means concentrating on particular stimuli and filtering out others. Attending to two or more tasks at once is divided attention, and keeping focus over a long time is sustained attention.

questions.stem: At a noisy party, Ana is focused on her conversation with a friend, yet she immediately notices when someone across the room says her name. This illustrates:
options: inattentional blindness, through missing a stimulus
selective attention, through the cocktail party effect
divided attention, through doing two tasks at once
sustained attention, through focusing for a long time
questions.explanation: The cocktail party effect shows that while we selectively attend to one conversation, some unattended information, such as our own name, is still processed and can capture attention. Ana is not deliberately doing two tasks, so this is not divided attention.

questions.stem: Which pair of tasks would most people find easiest to perform at the same time?
options: walking along a footpath and chatting with a friend
writing an essay and talking on the phone to a friend
listening to two different conversations at once
reading a novel and listening to a podcast story
questions.explanation: Divided attention is easiest when at least one task is automatic, like walking for most adults, and the tasks use different kinds of processing. The other pairs involve two controlled tasks that both draw on language, which compete for the same limited attention.

questions.stem: An experienced driver can chat easily while driving on a familiar road, but stops talking when heavy rain begins. The best explanation is that:
options: sustained attention improves in rain, so the driver focuses on the road
the rain activates selective attention, which blocks all sound
driving becomes an automatic task, which needs no attention at all
driving becomes a controlled task, leaving less attention for talking
questions.explanation: In familiar conditions, driving is largely automatic and needs little attention, so attention can be divided with talking. Heavy rain makes driving a controlled task that demands more attention, so the driver has less to spare.

questions.stem: An airport security officer screening bags on a monitor begins to miss more items as her shift goes on. This is best explained by a decline in:
options: sustained attention
divided attention
selective attention
top-down processing
questions.explanation: Sustained attention is maintaining focus on a task over a long period, and performance tends to fall the longer a monotonous task goes on. Divided attention would apply if she were doing more than one task at once, which the scenario does not describe.

questions.stem: In a well-known study, participants counting basketball passes often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the game. This shows that:
options: bottom-up processing ensures any unusual stimulus will always be noticed
selective attention can stop people noticing unexpected stimuli in plain view
divided attention lets people count passes while tracking every other event
sustained attention fails within a few seconds of starting a counting task
questions.explanation: Focusing on the passes meant other stimuli were filtered out, so many missed the gorilla, an effect called inattentional blindness. If unusual stimuli were always noticed through bottom-up processing, nobody would have missed it.

questions.stem: Perception is best described as the process of:
options: sending neural impulses from the sense organs to the brain
organising and interpreting sensory information to give it meaning
detecting a stimulus with the receptor cells of a sense organ
converting a stimulus into electrical impulses in the nervous system
questions.explanation: Perception is the psychological process of making sense of sensory information. Detecting a stimulus and converting it into neural impulses are parts of sensation, which comes before perception.

questions.stem: Bottom-up processing is perception that:
options: relies on the context in which the stimulus appears
occurs only when the stimulus is already familiar
begins with the features of the stimulus and builds up to a whole
begins with expectations and past experience to interpret a stimulus
questions.explanation: Bottom-up processing is driven by the data: the brain starts with basic features, such as lines and edges, and assembles them into a perception. Using expectations, past experience or context is top-down processing.

questions.stem: A pharmacist reads a doctor's messy handwriting by using the rest of the prescription to work out an unclear word. The pharmacist is mainly using:
options: bottom-up processing
divided attention
sustained attention
top-down processing
questions.explanation: Top-down processing uses knowledge, expectations and context to interpret unclear sensory information. Bottom-up processing would rely only on the shapes of the letters, which are not clear enough on their own.

questions.stem: Which example relies most on bottom-up processing?
options: examining the lines and angles of an unfamiliar abstract shape to work out what it is
reading a word with a missing letter by using the meaning of the surrounding sentence
spotting a friend quickly in a crowd at a café where you expected to meet her
seeing a face in the clouds because you have been thinking about your family
questions.explanation: When a stimulus is unfamiliar, there is little prior knowledge to draw on, so perception is built up from its features. Using a sentence's meaning, expecting a friend or seeing what is on your mind all apply prior knowledge, which is top-down processing.

questions.stem: Which depth cue requires the use of both eyes?
options: linear perspective
interposition
accommodation
retinal disparity
questions.explanation: Retinal disparity is a binocular cue: each eye receives a slightly different image, and the brain combines them to judge depth. Accommodation involves the lens of a single eye changing shape, so it is a monocular cue.

questions.stem: As a tennis ball approaches, Sasha's eyes turn inwards to follow it, and her brain uses the tension in her eye muscles to judge its distance. This depth cue is:
options: texture gradient
convergence
accommodation
retinal disparity
questions.explanation: Convergence is the inward turning of both eyes to focus on a near object; more strain signals that the object is closer. Accommodation is the change in the shape of the lens within each eye, not the turning of the eyes.

questions.stem: Why is accommodation classed as a monocular depth cue, while convergence is classed as binocular?
options: Accommodation happens in the lens of each eye; convergence needs both eyes to turn inwards
Accommodation needs both eyes to turn inwards; convergence happens in the lens of each eye
Accommodation is a pictorial cue in images; convergence is a physical cue in the body
Accommodation works only for far objects; convergence works only for objects far away
questions.explanation: In accommodation, the lens of each eye changes shape to focus, so one eye is enough. Convergence depends on the two eyes turning towards each other, so it requires both. Both are physiological cues used for near objects, not pictorial cues.

questions.stem: Railway tracks appear to come together in the distance. Which depth cue does this illustrate?
options: linear perspective
texture gradient
interposition
relative size
questions.explanation: Linear perspective is the apparent convergence of parallel lines as they recede into the distance. Texture gradient is the way surface detail becomes finer and denser with distance, which is a different pictorial cue.

questions.stem: In a photo of a beach, the pebbles in the foreground look large and distinct, while those further away look smaller and more tightly packed. This depth cue is:
options: texture gradient
linear perspective
height in the visual field
convergence
questions.explanation: A texture gradient is the change in detail of a surface, which becomes finer and denser the further away it is. Convergence cannot apply to a flat photo, because it depends on the eyes turning towards a real near object.

questions.stem: As a classroom door swings open, its image on the retina becomes a trapezium, yet Jordan still perceives it as rectangular. This is an example of:
options: size constancy
brightness constancy
the Gestalt principle of closure
shape constancy
questions.explanation: Shape constancy is perceiving an object as keeping its shape despite changes to the shape of its retinal image. Size constancy concerns objects appearing the same size as their distance changes, which is not what changes here.

questions.stem: A circle with a small gap in it is usually perceived as a complete circle. This illustrates the Gestalt principle of:
options: similarity
figure-ground
closure
proximity
questions.explanation: Closure is the tendency to fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole figure. Proximity is grouping elements that are close together, which does not explain filling in a missing section.

questions.stem: A perceptual set is:
options: a readiness to perceive a stimulus in a particular way
a group of depth cues that the brain uses together to judge distance
the set of receptors that detects a stimulus
a visual illusion that tricks the eyes
questions.explanation: A perceptual set is a predisposition, shaped by factors such as context, past experience, motivation and emotion, to perceive something in a certain way. Depth cues are biological and environmental information, not an expectation held by the perceiver.

questions.stem: In Bruner and Minturn's study, an ambiguous figure was seen as the number 13 when shown among numbers, but as the letter B when shown among letters. Which factor influenced perception?
options: motivation
emotional state
binocular depth cues
context
questions.explanation: The surrounding stimuli created a context that set participants to perceive the same figure as a number or a letter. Motivation is about needs and desires, such as hunger, which did not differ between the two conditions.

questions.stem: Hungry participants were more likely than recently fed participants to interpret blurry, ambiguous images as food. This shows the influence of:
options: culture on visual perception
retinal disparity on visual perception
motivation on visual perception
context on visual perception
questions.explanation: Motivation, such as hunger, can create a perceptual set to see stimuli related to the need. Both groups saw the same images in the same setting, so context does not explain the difference.

questions.stem: Some studies found that people raised in environments with few straight lines and right angles were less susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion. What does this suggest?
options: The Müller-Lyer illusion works through taste as well as through vision
Experience in a person's cultural environment can influence visual perception
Susceptibility to visual illusions is inherited and so cannot be changed
Some groups have better eyesight, which lets them see through the illusion
questions.explanation: The finding suggests that growing up surrounded by buildings with straight edges and corners shapes how people interpret line drawings, which is a social and cultural factor. The illusion depends on how the brain interprets the lines, not on eyesight, so better vision would not explain it.

questions.stem: Which list gives the five basic tastes?
options: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami
sweet, sour, salty, bitter and spicy
sweet, sour, savoury, bitter and minty
sweet, salty, bitter, fatty and spicy
questions.explanation: The five basic tastes detected by taste receptors are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (savoury). Spiciness from chilli is detected by pain and heat receptors, not taste receptors, so it is not a basic taste.

questions.stem: With a blocked nose from a cold, Joel finds that his favourite meal tastes bland. The best explanation is that:
options: a cold destroys the taste buds on the tongue
taste receptors are located inside the nose
the cold virus makes food chemically different
flavour depends on smell as well as on taste
questions.explanation: Flavour is the combined perception of taste and smell, so losing smell makes food seem bland even though the taste receptors on the tongue still work. A cold does not destroy taste buds.

questions.stem: Many older people find that food tastes blander than it used to. This is best explained by the biological factor of:
options: expectations, as older people expect food to taste bland
memory, as older people forget how food used to taste
age, as taste receptors decline in number and sensitivity
culture, as older people have lived with different cuisines
questions.explanation: Ageing reduces the number and sensitivity of taste receptors, and often the sense of smell, which is a biological change. Culture and expectations are social and psychological factors, so they do not answer a question about biology.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a psychological factor influencing gustatory perception?
options: a genetic sensitivity to the bitter taste of certain vegetables
eating meals with family members who regularly cook spicy food
expecting a drink to taste of strawberry because it is coloured red
the number of taste receptors a person has on their tongue
questions.explanation: Expectations created by appearance are psychological factors that can change how something tastes. The number of receptors and genetic sensitivity are biological factors, and the family's eating habits are a social factor.

questions.stem: Ravi grew up in a family that ate chilli at most meals, and as an adult he enjoys very spicy food that his friends find unpleasant. This is best explained by:
options: a biological factor, through his having fewer taste receptors
a psychological factor, through the perceptual set of hunger
a perceptual distortion, through his being a supertaster
a social factor, through his cultural and family experiences
questions.explanation: Repeated exposure to particular foods within a family and culture shapes food preferences, so this is a social factor. Supertasters tend to find strong flavours more intense and less pleasant, so being a supertaster would make spicy food harder, not easier, to enjoy.

questions.stem: In one study, participants rated the same wine as tasting better when told it was expensive than when told it was cheap. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Expectations can influence gustatory perception even when the stimulus is the same
Expensive wines contain more chemicals that activate the taste receptors
Gustatory perception is determined only by the chemicals in the food or drink
Participants could detect the difference in quality between the two wines
questions.explanation: Because the wine was identical, the difference in ratings must have come from the price information, a psychological factor creating an expectation. The claim that taste depends only on the chemicals cannot be right, because the chemicals did not change.

questions.stem: A visual illusion is best described as:
options: a consistent misinterpretation of real sensory information
an image of something that is not physically present
a fault in the eye that blurs the image on the retina
a random perceptual error that occurs only when a person is very tired
questions.explanation: In a visual illusion, the brain consistently misinterprets a real stimulus, and the effect persists even when we know it is wrong. Perceiving something that is not present at all is a hallucination, not an illusion.

questions.stem: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, the two lines produce retinal images of the same length, but one line looks longer. What does this show?
options: The lines are perceived only through bottom-up processing
The illusion works only for people who do not know about it
The difference is created by how the brain interprets the image
The eyes record the lengths of the two lines inaccurately
questions.explanation: Because the retinal images are equal, the error must arise in perception, when the brain interprets the lines in the light of the fins attached to them. The illusion persists even when people know the lines are equal, so knowing about it does not remove it.

questions.stem: In the Ames room, a person appears to grow or shrink as they walk from one corner to the other. The illusion occurs mainly because:
options: the room's lighting changes brightness as the person walks across
the viewer uses both eyes to judge the distance very accurately
the brain assumes the room is rectangular when it is actually distorted
the person really does change height because the floor slopes steeply upwards
questions.explanation: The Ames room is built in a distorted shape but looks rectangular from the viewing point, so the brain assumes both corners are the same distance away and misjudges the person's size. The illusion is viewed through a peephole with one eye, so binocular cues are not available to correct it.

questions.stem: Agnosia is a condition in which a person:
options: ignores one side of space after damage to the brain
cannot recognise stimuli despite their senses working normally
cannot detect any light because the retina is damaged
experiences one sense automatically when a different sense is stimulated
questions.explanation: Agnosia is a loss of the ability to recognise objects, faces or other stimuli, usually after brain damage, even though the sense organs work. Experiencing one sense when another is stimulated is synaesthesia, and ignoring one side of space is spatial neglect.

questions.stem: After a brain injury, Leo can see his wife's face clearly but does not recognise her until she speaks. Leo most likely has:
options: spatial neglect
synaesthesia
colour blindness
prosopagnosia
questions.explanation: Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, is a type of agnosia in which a person cannot recognise familiar faces, so they rely on cues such as voice. Leo has no difficulty seeing the face, so this is a problem of recognition rather than vision.

questions.stem: Sarah can describe the shape and colour of an object in front of her and can copy a drawing of it, but she cannot name it until she holds it. Which best explains this?
options: damage to her retinas, as the image of the object is not being formed
spatial neglect, as she is ignoring the side of space the object is on
prosopagnosia, as she is unable to recognise any objects she looks at
visual agnosia, as vision is intact but visual recognition is impaired
questions.explanation: Sarah's accurate description and copying show that she sees the object, and naming it by touch shows she knows what it is, so the problem is in recognising it by sight. Prosopagnosia is specific to faces, so it does not describe a difficulty recognising objects.

questions.stem: A supertaster is a person who:
options: is unable to detect bitter tastes because of a genetic difference
experiences tastes, especially bitter tastes, more intensely than most
can detect more than the five basic tastes that others can perceive
has learnt through training to identify very subtle flavours in food
questions.explanation: Supertasters perceive tastes, particularly bitterness, with greater intensity, a difference that is largely genetic. They do not detect extra basic tastes, and expert tasters who train their judgement are not necessarily supertasters.

questions.stem: Compared with other people, supertasters typically have:
options: a larger olfactory bulb that strengthens their sense of smell
more fungiform papillae, and so more taste buds, on the tongue
fewer fungiform papillae, and so fewer taste buds, on the tongue
taste receptors that respond only to sweet and salty chemicals
questions.explanation: Supertasters have a higher density of fungiform papillae, which hold taste buds, so they receive stronger taste signals. Having fewer papillae is characteristic of people who taste less intensely than average.

questions.stem: Which is a likely consequence of being a supertaster?
options: disliking bitter vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts
preferring very strong black coffee without milk or sugar
being unable to detect the sweetness in fruit and desserts
adding extra salt to most meals because food seems to taste rather bland
questions.explanation: Because supertasters find bitterness especially intense, many avoid bitter foods such as some green vegetables and black coffee. Finding food bland and adding extra salt is more typical of people with a reduced sense of taste.

questions.stem: After chewing a miracle berry, Amira finds that a lemon tastes sweet. This happens because the miraculin in the berry:
options: blocks every taste receptor, so only the smell of the lemon remains
adds a large amount of sugar to the lemon juice in the mouth
permanently destroys the receptors that detect sour tastes
binds to sweet receptors and activates them when the mouth is acidic
questions.explanation: Miraculin attaches to the sweet receptors on the tongue and activates them in acidic conditions, so sour foods are perceived as sweet. The effect is temporary and the lemon is chemically unchanged, so the receptors are not destroyed and no sugar is added.

questions.stem: What does the effect of miraculin show about the fallibility of gustatory perception?
options: Taste perception can change even when the chemicals in the food do not
Taste perception always gives an accurate account of a food's chemistry
Taste perception depends only on top-down expectations about the food
Taste perception is unaffected by changes to the taste receptors
questions.explanation: The lemon is just as acidic, yet it is perceived as sweet, showing that gustatory perception can misrepresent the stimulus. The change comes from altered receptor activity, a biological process, rather than from expectations, so it is not purely top-down.

questions.stem: When white wine was dyed red, many wine experts described it using terms normally used for red wine. This suggests that in judging flavour:
options: taste receptors are directly affected by the colour of a drink
experts are less influenced by expectations than non-experts
the red dye changed the chemical flavour of the white wine
visual information can override information from taste and smell
questions.explanation: The wine's chemistry was unchanged by the flavourless dye, so the experts' descriptions were driven by the colour they saw, a top-down influence on flavour judgement. Colour is detected by the eyes, not by taste receptors, so the receptors themselves were unaffected.

questions.stem: Synaesthesia is a condition in which:
options: stimulation of one sense automatically triggers an experience in another
a person cannot recognise familiar objects even though their vision is normal
a person ignores everything on one side of their visual field
a person experiences tastes far more intensely than average
questions.explanation: In synaesthesia, the senses become linked, so that, for example, hearing music or seeing letters triggers experiences of colour. Not recognising objects despite normal vision is agnosia.

questions.stem: For Hamish, the letter A always appears red and the number 7 always appears green, even when printed in black ink. This is an example of:
options: synaesthesia
visual agnosia
a visual illusion
spatial neglect
questions.explanation: Linking letters or numbers to specific colours is grapheme-colour synaesthesia, the most commonly studied form. A visual illusion misinterprets the stimulus itself, whereas Hamish perceives the letter correctly and also experiences a colour.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes synaesthesia from simply imagining or associating colours with letters?
options: The experiences are automatic and consistent over time
The experiences can be switched on and off at will
The experiences vary each time the letters are seen
The experiences occur only after brain damage in adults
questions.explanation: Synaesthetic experiences happen involuntarily and the same pairings stay consistent when the person is tested months or years apart. Imagined associations can be switched on and off and tend to change, which is what research tests to tell them apart.

questions.stem: Spatial neglect is a condition in which a person:
options: cannot recognise faces, even those of close family
sees colours when hearing particular sounds or words
is blind in both eyes after damage to the occipital lobe
fails to attend to one side of space, usually the left
questions.explanation: In spatial neglect, a person ignores stimuli on one side of space, most often the left after damage to the right hemisphere. Being unable to recognise faces is prosopagnosia, a different condition.

questions.stem: After a stroke, Joan eats only the food on the right side of her plate and shaves only the right side of her face. Which brain area is most likely damaged?
options: left parietal lobe
left temporal lobe
right frontal lobe
right parietal lobe
questions.explanation: Neglect of the left side most commonly follows damage to the right parietal lobe, which is involved in attending to space. Damage to the left parietal lobe would be more likely to cause neglect of the right side, which is the side Joan does attend to.

questions.stem: Why is spatial neglect considered a problem of attention rather than of vision?
options: The person can see the neglected side but chooses to ignore it deliberately
Information from the neglected side reaches the brain but is not attended to
The eyes cannot detect any light coming from the neglected side of space
The occipital lobe has been damaged, so no visual information is processed
questions.explanation: People with spatial neglect can often see on the neglected side, and the information still reaches the brain, but they fail to notice or respond to it. The neglect is not a deliberate choice; the person is unaware of what they are missing.
